lessons.title: Inside a computer: CPU, RAM, storage
lessons.summary: Know what each component does and which one is the bottleneck for a given problem.
points: The CPU executes instructions; more cores help parallel work, higher clocks help single-thread speed.
RAM is fast, volatile working memory; running out causes swapping, which is dramatically slower.
SSDs (NVMe) are orders of magnitude faster than HDDs for random access; HDDs are cheap bulk storage.
The motherboard, PSU and cooling decide what you can actually run reliably.

quiz.q: Your laptop slows to a crawl when you open many tabs and the disk light stays on. Most likely cause?
options: RAM exhausted and swapping to disk

lessons.title: Operating systems & the command line
lessons.summary: Processes, files, permissions and the shell are the daily tools of every engineer.
points: A process is a running program; the OS schedules processes onto CPU cores.
Everything is a file on Linux: devices, sockets, processes (/proc).
chmod/chown and users/groups control who can read, write or execute.
Pipes (|) compose small tools: grep, sort, uniq, awk, jq.

quiz.q: Which command shows the processes consuming the most CPU interactively?

lessons.title: How data is represented: bits, bytes, encodings
lessons.summary: Binary, hex, endianness, Unicode and floating point explain countless real-world bugs.
points: Everything is bits; hex is a compact way to read bytes.
Floating point is approximate: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in binary.
UTF-8 is variable-width and ASCII-compatible; a character is not always a byte.
Endianness decides byte order in memory and on the wire (network order is big-endian).

quiz.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in most languages?
options: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly

resources.title: Nand2Tetris: build a computer from NAND gates

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy, caches & performance
lessons.summary: Why locality of reference often matters more than clever algorithms.
points: Registers > L1/L2/L3 cache > RAM > SSD > network; each step is ~10-100x slower.
Sequential access is cache-friendly; pointer chasing is not.
Virtual memory gives each process its own address space via paging.
Measure with a profiler before optimising; hardware effects surprise everyone.

quiz.q: Iterating a 2-D array row-by-row vs column-by-column in C can differ hugely in speed mainly because of:

lessons.title: GPUs, accelerators & why AI needs them
lessons.summary: SIMD/SIMT parallelism, VRAM limits and the economics of AI hardware.
points: GPUs run thousands of lightweight threads: ideal for matrix multiplication.
VRAM capacity often limits model size more than raw compute.
Memory bandwidth, not FLOPs, is frequently the real bottleneck for LLM inference.
TPUs/NPUs are specialised accelerators; software stacks (CUDA, ROCm) matter as much as silicon.

quiz.q: For LLM inference, which resource is commonly the limiting factor?

lessons.title: Virtualization, containers & firmware basics
lessons.summary: Hypervisors, namespaces/cgroups and how a machine boots.
points: VMs virtualise hardware; containers share the host kernel using namespaces and cgroups.
Boot flow: firmware (UEFI) -> bootloader -> kernel -> init/systemd.
Hardware security: TPMs, secure boot, and why firmware updates matter.
Observability starts at the host: CPU steal, load, I/O wait, thermal throttling.

quiz.q: What do containers share with the host?

lessons.title: Programming fundamentals with Python
lessons.summary: Variables, control flow, functions and data structures: the universal core.
points: Types, variables, conditionals and loops are the same idea in every language.
Functions give names to behaviour and enable reuse and testing.
Lists, dicts and sets cover most everyday data-structure needs.
Read errors top-to-bottom: the last lines tell you what, the stack trace tells you where.

quiz.q: Which structure gives average O(1) lookup by key in Python?

lessons.title: Git & collaboration workflow
lessons.summary: Version control, branches and pull requests are non-negotiable professional skills.
points: Commits are snapshots; branches are cheap pointers to commits.
Small, focused commits with clear messages make review and debugging easy.
Pull requests + code review + CI are how teams ship safely.
Never commit secrets; rotate any key that leaks.

quiz.q: What is the safest response to accidentally committing an API key?
options: Delete the file in the next commit
Ignore it if the repo is private

lessons.title: Data structures, algorithms & Big-O
lessons.summary: Choose the right structure; reason about growth, not stopwatch time.
points: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size.
Hash maps, heaps, trees and graphs cover most interview and real-world needs.
Sorting and binary search: know the complexity and when to rely on the standard library.
Premature optimisation is the root of bugs; profile first.

quiz.q: Binary search on a sorted array of n items runs in:

lessons.title: Web fundamentals: HTML, CSS, JavaScript & HTTP
lessons.summary: The browser is the world's most deployed runtime.
points: HTML structures content, CSS presents it, JavaScript adds behaviour.
HTTP is request/response: methods, status codes, headers, cookies.
The DOM is a tree; render with textContent, not innerHTML, for untrusted data.
Accessibility (semantic HTML, focus, contrast) is part of quality, not an extra.

quiz.q: Which is the safest way to show user-supplied text in the DOM?

lessons.title: Testing, design & clean architecture
lessons.summary: Tests, modularity and boundaries keep systems changeable.
points: Unit tests are fast and isolated; integration tests check seams; a few end-to-end tests guard journeys.
Separate pure logic from I/O so most code is trivially testable.
Prefer composition, small interfaces and explicit dependencies.
Refactor continuously under test coverage; avoid big-bang rewrites.

quiz.q: Why separate pure logic from I/O?
options: It makes logic easy to test without mocks

lessons.title: Secure coding & the OWASP Top 10
lessons.summary: Injection, broken access control and supply-chain risk are the usual suspects.
points: Never build SQL/shell/HTML by string concatenation; use parameters and encoders.
Authorisation must be checked server-side on every request.
Pin and audit dependencies; least privilege for tokens and CI.
Log security events, never secrets.

quiz.q: The standard defence against SQL injection is:

lessons.title: How the internet works: IP, DNS, ports
lessons.summary: Follow a request from the browser to a server and back.
points: IP addresses locate hosts; ports locate services on a host.
DNS maps names to IPs and is cached at many layers.
Routers forward packets hop by hop; NAT lets many devices share one public IP.
Tools: ping, traceroute, dig, curl -v.

quiz.q: Which tool resolves a hostname to IP addresses?

lessons.title: The OSI & TCP/IP models
lessons.summary: Layers explain where a problem lives.
points: Link, Internet, Transport, Application are the working layers of TCP/IP.
TCP gives reliable ordered streams; UDP is lightweight and unordered.
Switches work on MAC addresses (L2), routers on IPs (L3).
Debug bottom-up: cable/Wi-Fi, IP, DNS, port, application.

quiz.q: Which protocol is typically chosen for low-latency streaming where occasional loss is acceptable?

resources.title: Cloudflare: What is the OSI model?

lessons.title: HTTP, TLS & HTTPS in depth
lessons.summary: What actually happens when you type https://...
points: TLS handshake negotiates keys and verifies the server certificate chain.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP).
Know status classes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
Caching headers (Cache-Control, ETag) are a free performance win.

quiz.q: A 502 status code most likely means:
options: A gateway got an invalid response from upstream

lessons.title: Subnets, CIDR, routing & VPNs
lessons.summary: Plan address space and understand private networks.
points: CIDR notation /24 means the first 24 bits are the network (256 addresses).
Routing tables pick the most specific matching route.
VPNs and overlays connect private networks securely over the internet.

quiz.q: How many addresses are in a /24 IPv4 block?

lessons.title: Load balancing, CDNs & reliability
lessons.summary: Scale and protect services at the edge.
points: L4 vs L7 load balancers: connection-level vs request-aware routing.
CDNs cache close to users; cache keys and invalidation are the hard parts.
Health checks, timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers prevent cascades.
DDoS mitigation = absorb at the edge + rate limit + autoscale.

quiz.q: Retries without backoff during an outage can cause:
options: A retry storm that worsens the outage

lessons.title: Network security & packet analysis
lessons.summary: Firewalls, zero trust and reading traffic with Wireshark.
points: Default-deny firewalls and least-privilege network policy shrink the blast radius.
Zero trust: authenticate and authorise every request, not just the perimeter.
Wireshark/tcpdump reveal handshakes, retransmits and DNS failures.
Keep software patched; follow CISA advisories for actively exploited bugs.

quiz.q: Which tool captures and inspects packets?

lessons.title: What is AI/ML? Core concepts
lessons.summary: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning in plain terms.
points: ML learns patterns from data instead of hand-written rules.
Training fits parameters; inference uses them; evaluation uses held-out data.
Overfitting: great on training data, poor on new data.
Garbage in, garbage out: data quality beats model cleverness.

quiz.q: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on test data. This is:

lessons.title: Python for data & your first model
lessons.summary: NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn/PyTorch basics.
points: Vectorised array operations are faster and clearer than loops.
Split data into train/validation/test before looking at results.
Start with a simple baseline; complexity must earn its place.
Track experiments so results are reproducible.

quiz.q: Why keep a separate test set?
options: To get an unbiased estimate of real-world performance

lessons.title: Neural networks & transformers
lessons.summary: How deep learning and attention power modern models.
points: Neurons compute weighted sums plus a non-linearity; backprop adjusts weights via gradients.
Transformers use self-attention to relate every token to every other token.
Pre-training on huge corpora then fine-tuning/aligning gives today's LLMs.
Scaling laws: more data, parameters and compute generally improve capability.

quiz.q: The key mechanism in a transformer is:

resources.title: arXiv: Attention Is All You Need

lessons.title: Prompting & building with the Claude API
lessons.summary: Reliable LLM features start with clear instructions, structure and evaluation.
points: Be specific: role, task, constraints, output format and examples.
Use system prompts for stable rules; keep untrusted content clearly separated.
Structured outputs (JSON schema) make responses machine-safe.
Stream long responses and always handle refusals, rate limits and max_tokens.

quiz.q: What should you do with text fetched from the web before acting on it?
options: Add it to the system prompt

lessons.title: RAG, tools & agents
lessons.summary: Give models knowledge and the ability to act, safely.
points: RAG: retrieve relevant chunks, then ground the answer in them with citations.
Tool use lets a model call functions; validate every tool input and constrain permissions.
Agents loop plan -> act -> observe; add budgets, timeouts and human approval for risky steps.
Prompt injection is the SQL injection of agents: never let retrieved content change the rules.

quiz.q: Best defence against prompt injection in agents?
options: Least-privilege tools, input validation and treating retrieved text as data

lessons.title: Evaluating, deploying & governing AI systems
lessons.summary: If you cannot measure it, you cannot improve it.
points: Build an eval set from real examples; track quality, cost and latency together.
Use LLM-as-judge carefully and spot-check with humans.
Monitor drift, add guardrails, log with privacy in mind.
Know licensing, safety and regulatory basics (e.g. NIST AI RMF).

quiz.q: What belongs in a good LLM eval set?
options: Representative real inputs incl. edge cases

lessons.title: Cloud fundamentals: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
lessons.summary: What the cloud is, what you rent, and who is responsible for what.
points: IaaS = virtual machines/networks; PaaS = managed runtimes; SaaS = finished software.
Shared responsibility: provider secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it.
Regions and availability zones are your blast-radius and latency tools.
Pay-as-you-go needs budgets and alerts from day one.

quiz.q: Under shared responsibility, who secures your application data and IAM policies?

lessons.title: Linux servers, SSH & Docker basics
lessons.summary: Package an app once, run it anywhere.
points: Images are immutable templates; containers are running instances.
A Dockerfile describes how to build the image; keep layers small and cache-friendly.
Never bake secrets into images; inject at runtime.
SSH keys beat passwords; disable password login.

quiz.q: Where should secrets live for a containerised app?
options: Injected at runtime via env/secret manager

lessons.title: CI/CD & Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary: Automate build, test, deploy and the infrastructure itself.
points: CI runs tests on every change; CD ships passing builds automatically.
Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation) makes environments reviewable and repeatable.
Use environments, approvals and rollbacks for safe releases.
Keep pipelines fast and secrets scoped with least privilege.

quiz.q: The main benefit of Infrastructure as Code is:

lessons.title: Cloud identity, storage & databases
lessons.summary: IAM, object storage and managed databases are the core building blocks.
points: IAM: least privilege, roles over long-lived keys, MFA for humans.
Object storage (S3-style) is durable and cheap; block storage backs VMs.
Managed databases handle backups and patching; you own schema, indexes and queries.
Encrypt at rest and in transit; classify data.

quiz.q: Prefer which for workloads calling cloud APIs?

lessons.title: Kubernetes & orchestration
lessons.summary: Run and heal containers at scale.
points: Pods are the smallest unit; Deployments manage replicas and rollouts.
Services and Ingress expose workloads; ConfigMaps/Secrets configure them.
Requests/limits, probes and autoscaling keep apps healthy and cost-aware.
Don't adopt Kubernetes until simpler platforms stop fitting.

quiz.q: What restarts a failed pod and keeps N replicas running?

lessons.title: Observability, SRE & cost control (FinOps)
lessons.summary: SLIs/SLOs, tracing and spend discipline.
points: Metrics, logs and traces answer 'is it broken, where, and why'.
SLOs and error budgets balance reliability with feature velocity.
Blameless postmortems turn incidents into improvements.
Tag resources, set budgets and right-size to stop silent cost creep.

quiz.q: An error budget is:
options: Allowed unreliability implied by an SLO
